newsitem.title: FRANCE: Angry Euro-MPs demand Bjerregaard resigns.
newsitem.headline: Angry Euro-MPs demand Bjerregaard resigns.

text.p: Green MEPs called on Wednesday for Environment Commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard to resign after she said the Commission could not accept vital European Parliament amendments to the fifth EU environment programme.
"After yesterday's debate on the Dybkjaer report, the Greens have completely lost the little confidence they had left in Ritt Bjerregaard," Swedish Green Per Gahrton said in a statement.
"She has neither the will nor the power to guarantee the fulfillment of the environmental goals as laid down in the fifth environmental action programme," the statement continued.

The last straw for the Euro-MPs came on Tuesday night when Bjerregaard acknowledged that at the present rate of progress, the EU was unlikely to meet its own targets for cutting pollution by the year 2000 and then said the Commission would not bring in new measures to ensure these goals were attained.
Euro-MPs, who were deeply disappointed with what they said were ineffectual and unambitious proposals for environmental protection, hauled the Commisson over the coals on Wednesday.
They adopted a report which poured scorn on the Commission's suggestions for reviewing and updating the 1992-2000 fifth European Union environmental action programme-- COM(95)647.

The report, drafted by Danish Liberal Dybkjaer, slammed the Commission for not proposing more action to tackle environmental problems, even though its own reports warned that the current approach was failing badly to prevent environmental degradation.
Euro-MPs complained that instead of coming up with specific plans and deadlines for reaching the 2000 targets, the Commission review just offered general guidelines.

This was not good enough and they demanded a string of amendments to turn the Commission proposal into something more ambitious, despite Bjerregaard's warning that the Commission would reject most of them.

The changes include a pledge to make current EU environmental standards as strict as current national norms in the three new EU states, Austria, Finland and Sweden -- a deal made before they joined the EU.

Euro-MPs also wanted additional practical measures to reduce emissions of CO2, NOx and VOCs and permissible levels of domestic waste and noise, and to stop pesticides and nitrates contaminating groundwater by 2005.

In the debate on Tuesday, Bjerregaard said she disagreed with Parliament on the purpose of the action programme review, although she acknowledged the need for more action, adding that this was largely the responsibility of the member states.
"(The Commission proposal) contains adjustments but it is not appropriate to prepare for the sixth environmental programme and set new goals and deadlines," she insisted.

Rapporteur Dybkjaer told Reuters recently she was not personally in conflict with the Danish commissioner, who was obliged to speak on behalf of the whole Commission and needed the Parliament to be firm on environmental issues to push decent legislation through.
The review of the fifth action plan needs the approval of both Parliament and ministers to come into force and Dybkjaer predicted reaching an agreement would be difficult.
